title_en: Suzhou Dingsheng Food Company v. Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce — dispute over administrative penalty for trademark infringement
ruling_gist_en: When determining whether a mark on a product constitutes trademark use, it is necessary to examine the specific manner in which the mark is used to see whether it has the function of identifying the source of goods or services. In the context of infringement of a registered trademark, trademark similarity should be confusing similarity, and whether market confusion is caused is one of the important factors in determining trademark similarity. Among them, whether market confusion is caused, under normal circumstances, includes not only actual confusion but also the likelihood of confusion. When an administrative authority for industry and commerce imposes administrative penalties on an administrative counterpart for trademark infringement in accordance with the law, it shall follow the principle of proportionality between punishment and fault, and exercise its discretion by comprehensively considering factors such as the degree of subjective fault of the person subject to the penalty, the circumstances, nature, consequences, and degree of harm of the illegal act. If the administrative authority for industry and commerce fails to consider the above factors that should be considered, violates the principle of proportionality between punishment and fault, and causes the result of the administrative penalty to be obviously unjust, the people's court has the power to change the penalty in accordance with the law.

full_text_en:
Suzhou Dingsheng Food Co., Ltd. v. Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce — Administrative penalty dispute over trademark infringement

[Ruling Summary]

In determining whether a mark on goods constitutes trademark use, it must be assessed based on the specific manner of use of the mark, i.e., whether it performs the function of identifying the source of goods or services. In the context of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark, similarity of trademarks shall mean confusing similarity, and whether market confusion is caused is one of the important factors in determining trademark similarity. Whether market confusion is caused generally includes not only actual confusion but also the likelihood of confusion. When an administrative authority for industry and commerce imposes an administrative penalty on an administrative counterpart for trademark infringement, it shall follow the principle of proportionality, comprehensively consider factors such as the degree of fault of the counterpart, the circumstances, nature, consequences, and degree of harm of the illegal act, and exercise its discretion accordingly. If the administrative authority for industry and commerce fails to consider the above factors and violates the principle of proportionality, resulting in an obviously unjust administrative penalty, the People's Court has the power to modify the penalty according to law.

Plaintiff: Suzhou Dingsheng Food Co., Ltd., domiciled at Shihu West Road, Wuzhong District, Suzhou, Jiangsu Province.

Defendant: Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce, Jiangsu Province, domiciled at Xujiang Road, Canglang District, Suzhou, Jiangsu Province.

Third Party: Donghua Textile Group Co., Ltd., domiciled at Gufang Middle Road, Wujin High-tech Industrial Development Zone, Changzhou, Jiangsu Province.

The Plaintiff, Suzhou Dingsheng Food Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "Dingsheng Company"), being dissatisfied with the administrative penalty imposed by the Defendant, Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce, Jiangsu Province (hereinafter referred to as "Suzhou AIC"), filed an administrative lawsuit with the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court.

The Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company, alleged: (1) The factual findings in the administrative penalty decision made by the Defendant, Suzhou AIC, were erroneous. Dingsheng Company's use of "LEHUO LOHAS" on its product packaging was not as a trademark, but as a product name and in accordance with the original meaning of the term. (2) The administrative penalty decision's finding that Dingsheng Company's use of "LEHUO LOHAS" on its product packaging constituted infringement did not comply with the provisions of the Trademark Law of the PRC. "LEHUO LOHAS" is a commonly used social term, and Dingsheng Company's fair use of another party's registered trademark would not mislead the public and should not be considered an infringing act under the Trademark Law. Therefore, Dingsheng Company requested the court to annul the Administrative Penalty Decision No. 00053 (2010) of Suzhou AIC and to order Suzhou AIC to bear the litigation costs of this case.

The Defendant, Suzhou AIC, argued: The facts found in the penalty imposed on the Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company, were clear and correct; the determination that Dingsheng Company's conduct constituted trademark infringement was in accordance with the law. Therefore, Suzhou AIC requested the court to dismiss Dingsheng Company's claims.

The Third Party, Donghua Company, stated: The facts stated in the administrative penalty decision in question were clear, the evidence was conclusive, the applicable law was correct, and the penalty was appropriate. Donghua Company requested the court to dismiss the Plaintiff Dingsheng Company's claims.

Upon trial at first instance, the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court found the following basic facts:

The Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company, is a wholly foreign-owned enterprise specializing in the production, processing (baking), and sale of baked goods and its own products. It had obtained registered trademarks: No. 3003766 and No. 4155628 for the "I Will" text and design mark (combined with Chinese characters "艾维尔"), No. 5063450 for the Chinese text mark "爱维尔", and No. 6289718 for the "爱维尔 I will" text and design mark, respectively in January 2003, September 2006, October 2008, and February 2010, all approved for use on goods in Class 30, including "cakes, bread, mooncakes, etc."

On June 23, 2009, the Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company, entered into an order contract with Zhejiang Jianli Packaging Co., Ltd., agreeing that Zhejiang Jianli Packaging Co., Ltd. would manufacture packaging products such as gift boxes, handbags, and individual packages bearing the mark at issue (hereinafter referred to as the "I will 爱维尔" combined with "LEHUO LOHAS" mark). In August 2009, Dingsheng Company began producing mooncakes, categorizing its mooncakes for that year into 23 categories, including "Qiushuang" (Autumn Fresh), "Meiman" (Happy), "Xingyue" (Star Moon), "Hexie" (Harmony), and the "LEHUO" category at issue, and produced corresponding advertising brochures. In early September 2009, Dingsheng Company placed these mooncakes on the market, primarily sold through 63 of Dingsheng Company's "I Will" (Aiweler) direct-sale stores and franchise stores within the Suzhou metropolitan area, via direct orders, and by temporarily hiring external personnel to sell gift vouchers. Dingsheng Company prominently displayed the combined "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS" mark at the lower left corner of the outer side of the handbags, inner liners, and individual mooncake packages of the "LEHUO" mooncakes in question, and also printed information such as the manufacturer's name (Dingsheng Company), telephone number, and factory address on both sides of the handbags.

The Third Party, Donghua Company, obtained the registered trademark No. 5345911 (hereinafter referred to as "LEHUO LOHAS") approved by the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce on July 14, 2009, approved for use on goods in Class 30: "pastries; instant rice; oatmeal; ice cream." It had not yet used the trademark on any products as of that time. On September 8, 2009, the Defendant, Suzhou AIC, received a report that the "LEHUO LOHAS" mooncakes produced and sold by the Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company, were suspected of trademark infringement, and accordingly initiated an investigation. The investigation revealed that among the 23 types of mooncakes produced and sold by Dingsheng Company in that year, one type used the "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark. According to the party's sales records, as of September 20, 2009, 10,200 boxes of "LEHUO LOHAS" mooncakes had been sold, at a listed price of RMB 119 per box, with a total value of RMB 1,213,800. Suzhou AIC held two hearings on this administrative penalty case on March 4, 2010, and April 12, 2010. On June 11, 2010, Suzhou AIC issued the Administrative Penalty Decision No. 00053 (2010), finding that Dingsheng Company's conduct fell under the provisions of Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law, constituting infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. Pursuant to Article 53 of the Trademark Law and Article 52 of the Implementing Regulations of the Trademark Law, Suzhou AIC ordered Dingsheng Company to cease the infringing act and imposed an administrative fine of RMB 500,000. After this specific administrative act was made, Dingsheng Company was dissatisfied and applied for administrative reconsideration with the Suzhou Municipal People's Government on June 29, 2010. The Suzhou Municipal People's Government, after review, held that the penalty decision by Suzhou AIC had clear factual findings, conclusive evidence, legal procedures, and appropriate content. On August 27, 2010, it issued the Administrative Reconsideration Decision No. [2010] Su Xing Fu Di 148, upholding the penalty decision No. 00053 (2010) made by Suzhou AIC. Dingsheng Company remained dissatisfied and subsequently filed an administrative lawsuit with the court.

Separately, regarding the origin and definition of the term "LEHUO" (乐活): "LEHUO" was coined by American sociologist Paul Ray in 1998, with its English meaning being "Lifestyles of Health and Sustainability." In August 2008, the Ministry of Education's "Report on the Language Situation in China (2006)" included "乐活族" (LEHUO Clan) as a new Chinese term.

At first instance, the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court held:

The Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company's use of the mark at issue constituted trademark use, and compared with the registered trademark "LEHUO LOHAS," the two were similar. The main dispute regarding whether this case constituted trademark infringement centered on whether confusion should be considered; however, if another party's use of a mark weakens or affects the connection, thereby substantially hindering the trademark owner's use of the registered trademark, confusion need not be considered. In this case, the "I Will" (Aiweler) brand had relatively strong recognition within a specific region. Dingsheng Company's extensive use of the mark at issue in that region would cause relevant consumers to establish a connection between "LEHUO LOHAS" and "I Will 爱维尔," thereby objectively severing the connection between Donghua Company and its registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark. Therefore, Dingsheng Company's use of "LEHUO LOHAS" infringed Donghua Company's exclusive right to use its registered trademark.

As to the Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company's argument during litigation that the Defendant, Suzhou AIC, had violated relevant provisions of the Administrative Penalty Law by holding multiple hearings, Suzhou AIC's holding of another hearing during the administrative penalty process, given the changes in factual findings and substantive judgments, did not violate any prohibitive provisions of the relevant law. Therefore, Dingsheng Company's claim of procedural defects in the administrative penalty lacked legal basis.

In conclusion, the Administrative Penalty Decision No. 00053 (2010) made by the Defendant, Suzhou AIC, had basically clear factual findings and legally correct application. The Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company's request to annul this penalty decision lacked factual and legal basis and was not supported.

Accordingly, pursuant to Article 56(4) of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC, the Suzhou Intermediate People's Court rendered the following judgment on July 20, 2011:

Reject all claims of the Plaintiff, Dingsheng Company.

Dingsheng Company was dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment and appealed to the Jiangsu High People's Court. The main grounds for appeal were: The first-instance judgment made errors in findings of fact. Dingsheng Company's use of "LEHUO LOHAS" on its mooncake series products was as a product style name. The first-instance court's finding that Dingsheng Company's use of "LEHUO LOHAS" constituted trademark use lacked legal and factual basis. As to whether relevant consumers were misled, the first-instance court excluded the important fact of whether confusion was caused, which was legally untenable. The registered trademark "LEHUO LOHAS" originated from a popular social term and had weak distinctiveness, giving others the right to fair use. Therefore, the first-instance judgment made errors in fact and in the application of law. Dingsheng Company requested the second-instance court to amend the judgment according to law and annul the Administrative Penalty Decision No. 00053 (2010).

The Appellee, Suzhou AIC, argued: The first-instance judgment clearly and correctly found the facts; Dingsheng Company's appeal was erroneous and should be dismissed.

The Appellee, Donghua Company, stated orally at the trial: The first-instance judgment clearly found the facts, had conclusive evidence, correctly applied the law, and followed legal procedures. Donghua Company requested the second-instance court to dismiss the appeal and uphold the original judgment.

Upon second-instance trial, the Jiangsu High People's Court confirmed the facts found at first instance.

The focus of the dispute in the second instance was: Whether the Administrative Penalty Decision No. 00053 (2010) made by the Appellee, Suzhou AIC, was lawful.

During the second-instance trial, the parties presented the following main arguments regarding the focus of the dispute.

The Appellant, Dingsheng Company, argued: (1) Dingsheng Company had already designed and printed packaging containing "LEHUO LOHAS" before Donghua Company obtained the trademark right, used it as a product style name for one of its 23 mooncake series for the Mid-Autumn Festival, and used it according to its original meaning—not as trademark use. (2) The trademark owner had not used the "LEHUO LOHAS" registered trademark on any goods, and no member of the public had indicated confusion about the source of goods due to the use of the allegedly infringing mark. (3) The registered trademark "LEHUO LOHAS" originated from a popular social term and had weak distinctiveness, giving others the right to fair use. (4) The Administrative Penalty Law does not provide for holding a second hearing; the Appellee, Suzhou AIC, violated relevant provisions by holding multiple hearings on the same case.

The Appellee, Suzhou AIC, argued: (1) "LEHUO LOHAS" is not a product name. The Appellant, Dingsheng Company, used "LEHUO LOHAS" in conjunction with "I will 爱维尔," and this mark objectively functioned to indicate the source of goods, serving as a trademark mark—constituting trademark use. (2) The prominent part of the mark used by Dingsheng Company was "LEHUO LOHAS," and compared with the registered trademark at issue, the overall combination was similar, constituting a similar trademark. (3) Dingsheng Company's use of "LEHUO LOHAS" did not constitute fair use, and its manner of use would mislead consumers. (4) Granting a party the right to a second hearing complies with the provisions of the Administrative Penalty Law.

The arguments of the Appellee, Donghua Company, were the same as its statements.

The Jiangsu High People's Court held in the second instance:

The Appellant, Dingsheng Company's use of the combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS" constituted trademark use. This mark was similar to Donghua Company's registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark, and its conduct infringed Donghua Company's exclusive right to use its registered trademark. The Appellee, Suzhou AIC's finding that Dingsheng Company's conduct constituted infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark, and its order to cease the infringing conduct, were correct administrative penalties. However, the imposition of a fine of RMB 500,000 was manifestly unfair. The specific reasons are:

(A) The Appellant, Dingsheng Company's use of the combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS" constituted trademark use.

A trademark is a mark used by a producer of goods or provider of services to distinguish their own goods or services from those of others, and it must possess distinctiveness and a distinguishing function. In determining whether a mark on goods constitutes trademark use, it must be assessed based on the specific manner of use of the mark, i.e., whether it performs the function of identifying the source of goods or services.

In this case, during the promotion of its 2009 Mid-Autumn Festival mooncakes, the Appellant, Dingsheng Company, categorized its mooncakes into 23 styles, including "Qiushuang," "Meiman," "Xingyue," "Hexie," and the "LEHUO" style in question. Although Dingsheng Company argued that "LEHUO LOHAS" was only used as a product name for one of its mooncake styles, based on the manner in which it was labeled on the mooncake packaging, the combined use of "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS" constituted trademark use. First, Dingsheng Company did not use its own "I Will" (Aiweler) series of registered trademarks in a standardized and prominent manner on its mooncake packaging. Second, in the combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS," "LEHUO LOHAS" was used in conjunction and integrated with "I will 爱维尔." Dingsheng Company did not emphasize its own trademark "I will 爱维尔"; instead, it highlighted "LEHUO LOHAS," resulting in a clear mark effect. Therefore, based on the actual use of the combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS," it could not be seen that "LEHUO LOHAS" was used as a style name under its registered trademark or the "I will 爱维尔" mark. The combined "LEHUO LOHAS" and "I will 爱维尔" mark functioned as a whole mark indicating the source of goods, constituting trademark use.

(B) The combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS" used by the Appellant, Dingsheng Company was similar to Donghua Company's registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark, and its conduct infringed the Appellee, Donghua Company's exclusive right to use its registered trademark.

Article 52(1) of the Trademark Law of the PRC provides that the use of a trademark identical or similar to a registered trademark on identical or similar goods without the permission of the trademark registrant constitutes infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark. In this case, the mooncakes on which the Appellant, Dingsheng Company used the disputed mark and the pastries and other goods for which the Appellee, Donghua Company's registered trademark was approved are similar goods, and the two trademarks are not identical—these points are not in dispute. Therefore, the key factor in determining whether Dingsheng Company's conduct constituted trademark infringement is whether the disputed mark used by Dingsheng Company and Donghua Company's registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark are similar.

Although the Trademark Law of the PRC does not specifically define the determination of trademark similarity, in judicial practice, it is generally recognized that trademark similarity means that the allegedly infringing trademark and the registered trademark are similar in terms of the shape, pronunciation, or meaning of their characters, or the composition and colors of their design, or the overall structure resulting from the combination of their elements, or similar in terms of their three-dimensional shape or color combination, such that it is easy for relevant consumers to mistake the source of the goods or believe that their source has a specific connection with the goods bearing the registered trademark. In other words, trademark similarity in the context of infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark shall mean confusing similarity, and whether market confusion is caused is one of the important factors in determining trademark similarity. Whether market confusion is caused generally includes not only actual confusion but also the likelihood of confusion. When specifically determining whether trademarks are similar, the following principles should be applied: first, take the general attention of relevant consumers as the standard; second, conduct both an overall comparison of the trademarks and a comparison of their key parts, and the comparison should be made with the compared objects isolated from each other; third, consider the distinctiveness and recognition of the registered trademark for which protection is sought. In this case, the disputed mark used by the Appellant, Dingsheng Company, compared with the Appellee, Donghua Company's registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark, should be found to constitute a similar trademark. The reasons are:

First, from an overall comparison, in the combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS" used by the Appellant, Dingsheng Company, "LEHUO LOHAS" was relatively prominent in the overall structure, occupying the main part. The shape, pronunciation, and meaning of the Chinese and English characters in this part were identical to those of Donghua Company's registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark, and their constituent elements were very close, making it easy for relevant consumers to mistake the source of the goods.

Second, considering the distinctiveness and recognition of the registered "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark, the two trademarks are likely to cause confusion and mistake among market relevant consumers:

(1) Although the term "乐活族" (LEHUO Clan) was included in the "Report on the Language Situation in China (2006)," as a new term that appeared in 2006, its inclusion only indicates that the term had a certain frequency of use and popularity during that period; it does not mean that the term had already reached the level of a commonly used term at that time. Even less can the popularity of the term during the litigation phase be used to retroactively conclude that at the time "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark was approved for registration in 2009, it had become a commonly used social term. Currently, the "LEHUO LOHAS" registered trademark has not been revoked, which also indicates that although the term "乐活" has a certain meaning, at the time of approval for registration, it had not reached the level of a commonly used term and had a certain degree of distinctiveness. Therefore, it should be found that the disputed mark used by Dingsheng Company served as a trademark identifier, rather than a description of the goods. When ordinary consumers see the combined mark "I will 爱维尔" and "LEHUO LOHAS," they would not understand it as the meaning "I will live healthily." The Appellant, Dingsheng Company's argument that "LEHUO LOHAS" is a commonly used social term and that its use was in accordance with its original meaning, constituting fair use, cannot be sustained.

Second, the "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark was approved for registration in July 2009. Although at the time the Appellee Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce investigated in September 2009 and issued the administrative penalty decision in June 2010, the registered trademark "LEHUO LOHAS" had no market recognition because it had not actually been used, and during the second instance proceedings of this case the registered trademark remained unused; nevertheless, since the "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark had just been approved for registration, the use by Appellant Dingsheng Company was investigated by the administrative authority for industry and commerce. Therefore, the determination of whether confusion exists between the two marks should take the time of the administrative investigation as the benchmark. In the absence of evidence that Appellee Donghua Company’s registration of the "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark was done with subjective intent of malicious preemptive registration, it is necessary to reserve a certain protective space for the trademark owner whose registered trademark has not yet been used. In such circumstances, the determination of confusion should focus more on the likelihood of confusion rather than whether actual confusion has occurred. In judicial practice, where the determination of trademark infringement based on likelihood of confusion uses actual confusion as the standard, there must ordinarily be special historical factors such as long-term good-faith use of the accused infringing trademark and the two marks having formed a state of coexistence in good faith. In this case, no such special historical factors exist. Although Dingsheng Company used the words "LEHUO LOHAS" for corresponding packaging design and commissioned production before the approval and registration of the trademark in question, such use was very brief, less than one month, and did not create a situation of coexistence in good faith due to long-term use of the two marks. If the mere fact that the registered trademark in question has not actually been used and will not cause actual confusion were consistently taken as the standard for infringement determination, it might unduly impact the trademark registration system and be detrimental to the protection of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark.

(III) The administrative penalty imposed by the Appellee Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce is manifestly unjust.

Manifestly unjust administrative penalty generally refers to a situation where the administrative penalty is not formally illegal, but the result of the penalty is clearly unfair, harming the lawful rights and interests of citizens, legal persons, or other organizations. Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Penalty Law of the PRC stipulates that the imposition of an administrative penalty must be based on facts and commensurate with the facts, nature, circumstances, and degree of social harm of the illegal act. Therefore, when imposing an administrative penalty, the administrative body shall follow the "principle of proportionality between penalty and fault" established by this provision. If the administrative penalty imposed by an administrative body clearly violates the principle of proportionality between penalty and fault, making the result of the administrative penalty disproportionate to the degree of illegality, it shall be deemed to be a manifestly unjust administrative penalty.

Article 53 of the Trademark Law of the PRC provides that, when dealing with disputes over infringement of the exclusive right to use a registered trademark, if the administrative department for industry and commerce determines that the infringement is established, it shall order the immediate cessation of the infringing act and may also impose a fine. The correct understanding of this provision is that when an administrative authority for industry and commerce imposes an administrative penalty for trademark infringement, while ordering the immediate cessation of the infringing act, it has the discretion to choose whether to also impose a fine. Therefore, in exercising this discretion, the administrative authority for industry and commerce shall, in accordance with the "principle of proportionality between penalty and fault" established in Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Penalty Law, comprehensively consider factors such as the subjective fault of the party subject to the penalty, the circumstances, nature, consequences, and degree of social harm of the illegal act, in deciding whether to impose a concurrent fine. In this case, the disputed mark used by Appellant Dingsheng Company was found to be similar to the registered trademark "LEHUO LOHAS" of Appellee Donghua Company, and its conduct constituted trademark infringement. The Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce, as the administrative authority responsible for investigating and handling infringements of the exclusive right to use registered trademarks, had the authority under the Trademark Law of the PRC to investigate and impose penalties for the illegal act. However, in ordering Dingsheng Company to cease the infringing act while concurrently imposing a fine of RMB 500,000, it failed to consider the following factors that should have been taken into account:

First, prior to the approval and registration of the "LEHUO LOHAS" registered trademark, Appellant Dingsheng Company had already undertaken corresponding packaging design and commissioned production, and Dingsheng Company lacked subjective malice in seeking to ride on the reputation of Appellee Donghua Company’s registered trademark.

Second, the "LEHUO LOHAS" trademark was approved for registration in July 2009, and the Appellee Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce investigated Appellant Dingsheng Company’s infringing conduct in September 2009 and issued the administrative penalty decision in June 2010. Because Dingsheng Company’s infringement period was very brief and the registered trademark in question had not yet been actually used, Dingsheng Company’s infringing conduct did not cause actual harm to the trademark owner, Donghua Company.

Third, from the perspective of the use of the combined mark "I will Aiwei'er" and "LEHUO LOHAS," Appellant Dingsheng Company only used the mark in the promotional activities for Mid-Autumn Festival mooncakes in 2009, and as one of the 23 series of mooncakes for that year’s Mid-Autumn Festival, Dingsheng Company did not engage in specialized, extensive, or substantial advertising for the mooncakes bearing the mark. Its sales model for the goods was also limited to sales at its own specialty stores or direct marketing. Moreover, because the registered trademark "LEHUO LOHAS" had no market recognition due to non-use, it had not caused actual confusion or misidentification among the relevant public in the market, so the infringement and its circumstances were clearly minor.

Based on the above factors, when the Appellee Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce imposed the administrative penalty on Appellant Dingsheng Company, ordering it to cease the infringing act should have been sufficient to achieve the administrative enforcement purpose of protecting the exclusive right to use the registered trademark and safeguarding the legitimate rights and interests of consumers and the relevant public. However, the Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce failed to consider factors such as Dingsheng Company’s absence of subjective fault, the clearly minor nature and circumstances of the infringement, and the fact that no actual harmful consequences had occurred, and concurrently imposed a fine of RMB 500,000 on Dingsheng Company, making the result of the administrative penalty manifestly disproportionate to the degree of social harm of the illegal act. The administrative penalty lacked appropriateness and necessity and shall be deemed a manifestly unjust administrative penalty.

Regarding Appellant Dingsheng Company’s contention that the Appellee Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce’s multiple hearings violated the relevant provisions of the Administrative Penalty Law and constituted procedural illegality, the court of second instance holds that the Administrative Penalty Law of the PRC provides for hearing procedures but does not explicitly stipulate the number of hearings. Therefore, the multiple hearings held by the Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce did not violate any prohibitory provisions of the relevant law. Dingsheng Company’s argument that the Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce committed procedural illegality lacks legal basis and is not supported.

In summary, the Jiangsu High People’s Court holds that when an administrative authority for industry and commerce imposes an administrative penalty on an administrative counterpart for trademark infringement in accordance with the law, it shall exercise its discretion in compliance with the principle of proportionality between penalty and fault. That is, while ensuring the realization of administrative management objectives, it shall also protect the lawful rights and interests of the administrative counterpart. The administrative penalty shall be limited to what is necessary to achieve the purpose and objective of administrative enforcement, and the rights and interests of the counterpart shall be minimized to the greatest possible extent. If the administrative authority for industry and commerce fails to consider factors that should be considered, violates the principle of proportionality, and causes the result of the administrative penalty to be manifestly unjust, the people’s court has the authority to render a judgment to change the penalty in accordance with the law. In this case, the administrative penalty imposed by the Appellee Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce was manifestly unjust and shall be changed. The judgment of first instance had clear factual findings and lawful trial procedures, but applied the law incorrectly and shall be revised accordingly. Therefore, in accordance with Article 52, Item (1) and Article 53 of the Trademark Law of the PRC, Article 4, Paragraph 2 of the Administrative Penalty Law of the PRC, and Article 54, Item (4) and Article 61, Item (2) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the PRC, the Jiangsu High People’s Court rendered the following judgment on July 31, 2012:

1. The administrative judgment of the Suzhou Intermediate People’s Court of Jiangsu Province, (2011) Su Zhong Zhi Xing Chu Zi No. 0001, is reversed;

2. The administrative penalty decision of the Suzhou Administration for Industry and Commerce of Jiangsu Province, Su Gong Shang An Zi (2010) No. 00053, dated June 11, 2010, which ordered "1. Cessation of the infringing act; 2. A fine of RMB 500,000," is changed to: "Cessation of the infringing act."

This judgment is final.
